name: soninké
catalog_citation: Creissels, Denis. 2016. Phonologie segmentale et tonale du soninké (parler du Kingi). Mandenkan 55: 3-174. PDF from author's site, http://www.deniscreissels.fr/public/Creissels-phon.soninke.pdf
catalog_locator: §3.2 'Ton haut et ton bas', p.28; §4 'Conclusion', p.76
catalog_quote: En faisant abstraction de la modulation descendante dont il sera question en 3.3, chaque syllabe d’un mot en soninké du Kingi est caractérisable comme ou bien haute (H) ou bien basse (B). On discutera plus loin la possibilité d’analyser ce système comme un système à ton bas marqué ... Une caractéristique remarquable de ce système tonal est que rien dans la distribution des tons ou dans les processus tonals ne demande de reconnaître des propriétés tonales différentes aux différents types de syllabes. Autrement dit, l’unité porteuse de ton coïncide avec la syllabe, sans distinction entre syllabes légères et syllabes lourdes. ... [p.76] Par ailleurs, pour essayer de rendre compte des propriétés tonales des formes nominales déterminées, il [Ousmane Moussa Diagana] a introduit des notions (ton moyen, accent) qui ne sont pas pertinentes pour décrire le système tonal soninké, et qui relevaient…
sweep_summary: Two title hits, neither readable online. (1) Borges 2009, Leiden MA thesis 'Some prosodic features of Soninke of Gambia', 121 pp.: print only (Leiden UB Closed Stack 3, 8553 A 42; OCLC 778344413; not in the Leiden student-theses repository, no Google Books preview). Relevance unclear from the title, but it is the only first-hand prosodic study of a western (Gambian) variety, and Creissels (2015 p.2, 2016 pp.5/27-28) says western varieties may have substantially different prosodic systems and Bakel may be losing tone — so high acquisition priority as a possible variety-level refinement. (2) Rialland 1991, Linguistique Africaine 7: 117-124, her reply to Creissels 1991 'Remarques sur le système tonal du soninké' defending Rialland 1990 'Le système prosodique du soninké' (HAL metadata only, keyword Tonology): a tonological debate on Kaédi Soninke, not a stress description; print only, low priority. Nothing found contradicts the 'tonal' coding. New first-hand text read: Creissels 2015 CALL paper (author's site) states 'Kingi Soninke has two contrastive level tones, H and L' with no stress/accent — confirms, does not supersede Creissels 2016. findings rest on Glottolog, HAL, Crossref, Leiden Primo, LPP, Google Books and Creissels' site downloads.

new_statements.quote: As illustrated in (4), Kingi Soninke has two contrastive level tones, H and L. (4a) LH vs. HH kàrá 'die' kárá 'break'; qòoró 'grow' qóoró 'pick up' (4b) HH vs. HL légé 'dance' légè 'catch fire'; qáwá 'get moist' qáwà 'be similar' [...] [p.2:] On the basis of the data I have at my disposal, a reasonable hypothesis is that the tonal system described in this presentation is at least substantially representative of the Eastern Soninke varieties (i.e. roughly speaking, the varieties located east of Kayes (Qàayí)). By contrast, the field work I had the opportunity to do in collaboration with Anna Marie Diagne on Bakel Soninke suggests that Western varieties may have substantially different prosodic systems.
new_statements.citation: Creissels, Denis. 2015. The inflectional role of tone in Soninke (West Mande). Paper/handout, 45th Colloquium on African Languages and Linguistics (CALL), Leiden, 31 Aug-1 Sep 2015, 16 pp. Author's site.
new_statements.locator: §3.1 'H vs. L', p. 4 (PDF p. 4 of 16); variety caveat §1, p. 2
new_statements.reading: First-hand (Kingi, eastern Soninke) two-level-tone analysis, H vs. L on every syllable with lexical minimal pairs, plus floating-L downstep; no word stress or accent is mentioned anywhere in the paper (no hits for 'stress'/'accent' in the text). Confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding; adds the explicit caveat that western varieties (Bakel, and by extension Gambian Soninke, the subject of Borges 2009) may have substantially different prosodic systems.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the Creissels 2016 PDF we hold at the stated places (§3.2 p.28; §4 p.76). (2) The deciding source is a 172-pp dedicated segmental-and-tonal phonology (2016) by Denis Creissels, first-hand data on three eastern varieties, reviewing all prior phonological literature; among Glottolog's 34 descriptive refs nothing later or more detailed on prosody exists (the 'grammars' are the Diagana theses 1980-1995, Kendall 1980 SIT handbook, Girier 1996, Diagne 2006/2008). (3) downloaded now: Diagne 2006 (open, Mainz; Bakel variety) and Y. Diagana 1990 (open scan, LLACAN; Kaédi) both independently analyse Soninke as a marked-Low two-tone system with floating tones and downstep and say nothing of word stress — confirming 'tonal, no stress rule stated' across western and eastern varieties; Y. sources.quote: Bakel Soninke data. Ch.6 analyses a tone system: roots carry a tonal plane, non-root morphemes are lexically toneless and get tone by spreading/floating-tone assignment/default H; three purely tonal morphemes (floating L 'complétude' suffix causing downstep or final falling contour; two L boundary prefixes). §6.2: 'Lexicalement le système soninké est à registre marqué bas' with lexical inventory H and L and a surface mid-high tone from downstep. No word stress/accent anywhere (the only 'accent' hit in the text is non-prosodic).
sources.locator: Introduction pp.3-4; ch.6 'Système tonal' pp.152-173, esp. §6.1.2-6.1.3 pp.153-154 and §6.2 pp.155-156

sources.quote: Kaédi Soninke. Sets out to derive 'les schèmes tonals de base des bases nominales, des morphèmes de nombre et des morphèmes de détermination'; determiners have invariant base tone schemes represented with H and B (e.g. ke /H/, tana /HB/), nominal bases show 'homotonalité' in generic/compound/adjectival phrases. Purely tonal analysis; no stress/accent.
